newsitem.title: USA: Sergeant accused of rape describes strict detention.
newsitem.headline: Sergeant accused of rape describes strict detention.

text.p: An Army sergeant accused of raping 10 women took the witness stand Friday to describe months of a regimented, shackled existence under maximum security detention while awaiting trial.

Staff Sgt. Delmar Simpson, charged with 129 counts of sexual misconduct and other crimes at the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground, was testifying at a pre-trial hearing regarding his lawyers' request to credit him with time served if he is convicted and sentenced.
The lawyers are seeking five days of credit for every day served, based on what they said were overly harsh conditions for someone who had not gone to trial.

Simpson, sporting a dress uniform and smooth-shaven head, said that during seven months of pre-trial detention at the Quantico Military Brig in Quantico, Virgina, he had spent 22 hours a day in a 6-by-8 foot cell, where he was not allowed to lie down from his 5 a.m. wake-up call until 6 in the evening.
"You can sit in your chair. You can stand, you can walk in your cell. That's all, sir," Simpson said in sombre tones as he described his confinement.

Breaks away from his cell included brief periods of "sunshine call" in which he was allowed to stand or sit outside, and a one-hour television break three times a week, he said. He was required to wear shackles during such breaks.

Asked about his treatment by prison guards, he said, "Some good, some bad," and described being cursed for leaving bread on his plate. He said he had not been allowed to see a chaplain for Easter or Christmas.

Prison commander Chief Warrant Officer James Hart testified that the conditions of Simpson's treatment were standard for a maximum-security detainee, and said high security was warranted because of the severity of charges against Simpson and because he was believed to be a flight risk.

"He did have a potential for violent behaviour, and until it's proven otherwise I think it's a very sound statement," Hart said. Simpson had not exhibited any behaviour problems during his confinement, he said.
He said the prison was not equipped to separate detainees awaiting trial under maximum security conditions from convicted prisoners.
Simpson's attorney, Capt. Edward Brady, said two legal officals at Aberdeen had requested the terms of Simpson's confinement be relaxed, but the requests were not acted on.

Before being brought to Aberdeen for the pre-trial hearings this week, Simpson had been held at Quantico from Sept. 11, Jury selection in the case is to begin Monday, and his trial is scheduled to start April 14.

Simpson is the only soldier, among 10 from Aberdeen charged in a major sexual misconduct scandal, to have been detained pending trial. Four of those cases have been resolved, and Simpson would be the first soldier charged in the scandal to go to trial.
The military judge in the case, Col. Paul Johnston, has not yet ruled on the request for credit. The request is "low on my priority of motions," he said in court.
